newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FOCUS-Belgian Cera Bank holds breath after good 96.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Belgian Cera Bank holds breath after good 96.

text.p: The Cera Bank group, Belgium's sixth-largest, said on Thursday that consolidated net profit soared 71 percent in 1996 but warned that it and other banks faced a tougher time ahead.
"Luckily every (bank) has recorded excellent 1996 results because we're facing a period which is going to cost us quite a bit of money," Cera chief executive officer Willy Breesch said.
Breesch told a news conference on 1996 earnings that the direct cost of the introduction of the euro for Belgian banks was 20 billion francs ($576 million) over the next four to five years.
In addition banks are likely to lose 20 billion francs a year due to the loss of forex trading commission income.
They will also incur costs in dealing with the millennium bug -- making sure their computers can handle the date changing from 1999 to 2000 without crashing.
"These operations also have a very big opportunity cost," said Breesch, who is also chairman of the Belgian Banking Association.
The fact that computer engineers would have to focus entirely on the euro and millennium bug would stop them from developing banks' other activities.
"All new commercial activities will have problems," he said.

The unlisted Cera Bank group had a 1996 consolidated net profit of 5.78 billion francs against 3.38 billion a year earlier, partly due to increased demand from investors for savings accounts and off-balance sheet instruments.
Provisions remained steady in 1996, although the bank said it set aside 521 million francs to cope with the introduction of the euro and the millenium bug.
Nearly half the 71.2 percent rise in earnings was due to a 45.8 percent rise in profit at parent company Cera Bank.

Cera also profited handsomely from its 44.5 percent stake in Belgian insurance company ABB (Insurance of the Belgian Farmers' Union). Cera's share in ABB profit rose to 1.225 billion francs from 500 million in 1995.
Own funds rose more than nine percent to 67.1 billion. Breesch noted the bank's balance sheet contained few subordinated loans.
"So we still have room to expand. Own funds can easily go up because we have quite a few possibilities via subordinated loans," he said.
Breesch said Cera was due to open its first office in the Dutch town of Maastricht in September and was also planning an acquisition in Switzerland before the summer.
Cera said its takeover of Banque Indosuez Belgium was on track and should be finalised in May. It agreed last December it would buy 80 percent of Banque Indosuez Belgique from French Banque Indosuez.
